per_item.reference: All three, then, and each one alone would have stalled it. The residues first: the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks are named as the slow rotting ones to avoid in the residue layer, and what should go there is the fast kind, chopped, being straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. The order second: the build is a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of chopped residues trodden down well, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. Tipped together, the manure and the activator are not where they do their work. The watering third: each layer is watered as it is laid, because water poured over a finished heap runs off the outside and leaves the middle dry, which is exactly what you found. Rebuild it that way, on a shaded site out of the wind and rain, and ask ICAT what to do with the stalks instead.

history.content: I built a heap last season and it never turned into anything.
Let me narrow it. Tell me what you put in it, in what order, and when you watered it. Those three are where the catalogue is most specific, and most heaps that fail have missed one of them.

draws.answer: Then two of the four are in the catalogue's own sequence and two are not. The stalks and the husks are the slower layer, 10 to 20 cm thick and never watered more than half, so you watered it as they came in rather than as a heap. The manure is the other half, about 30 cm, and it has to be watered as it goes: wet each layer as you lay it, in layers, so that it compacts rather than airing off. And the activator is not on the catalogue's list of four: topsoil, well rotted compost, or Mycotri, which is not a product at all. It gives the recipe and the stages, so check those against what you built. If water did not come with the manure, and you watered as it came in, then that was the thing that carried it.

Then two things to change, and one that costs you time. The catalogue names wood ash as one of the four things to apply in moderation, alongside topsoil, well rotted compost and manure, and it names topsoil and well rotted compost as the activator, so a heap of stalks and husks with nothing but a little topsoil is the one the catalogue warns about. The third is the watering: you water each layer as you lay it down, not the finished heap at the end. And the order, which it gives as two: a little wood ash on the topsoil, 10 to 20 cm of rice husks or ronier leaves, 5 cm of manure, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. So the heap stopped at the last layer, the one that will have been wet but not watered, and the rest was left out of the plan. That is the real problem.

Two hundred chicks calls for a chick room the size of a small building. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference size is one chick room of 50 square metres for 60 chicks, and that is the one you will be running. history.content: How can I tell the difference between stalk borer damage and maize streak virus in my field?

Also check for insects: borers appear as holes and a weakened stem, while virus shows no borer and the plant is stunted from chlorotic spots. If you see dead-heart with tunnels, it is stalk borer; if you see streaks along veins and no borer, it is maize streak virus. If you need help choosing the right variety, go to ICAT for the approved seed.

Dry the newly harvested maize until it becomes hard, about 13-14% moisture, so the kernels snap instead of dents, and then store the grain in an airy, dry store. First, clean the store and remove any residues from last season because larger grain borer can carry over. Then put the dried maize in sound, sealed bags or bins. Next, blend an approved grain protectant or dried neem-leaf powder evenly through the grain. If insects are still present, apply the approved storage insecticide at the labelled rate. For the correct insecticide product, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: Those symptoms are maize streak virus. Remove the worst-affected plants and destroy them to cut the source of infection. Do not use any spray because no spray cures an infected plant. Plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety next season and ask ICAT for the recommended seed. history.content: My maize leaves have chlorotic spots that turn into pale streaks along the veins and the plants look stunted. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs indicate maize streak virus, so rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source. Next season, request an improved MSV-tolerant variety from ICAT and plant it, keeping the field uniform and timely. Avoid late sowing because it raises infection chances. No spray can cure an infected plant, so remove the plants you can see. For confirmation and variety advice, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: Seven by four is 28 square metres, which is exactly the grower compartment in that reference's own worked layout: 28 square metres for 420 birds at 15 per square metre. That breeder half matches the reference's own figure of a compartment 4 m by 3.5 m for 140 birds. history.content: I want to know whether my building is big enough.

Give me two things: the inside measurements, and the ages of the birds you want to put in it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference works on 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for the growers, and the 2017 ESFT village compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre for the improved family henhouse, so I also need to know which of the two you are building.
Seven metres by four, the commercial model, and I want breeders and growers both.

draws.answer: Then the breeder compartment is 56 square metres and the grower compartments are 84 square metres, which is exactly the count the 2020 reference gives for one unit at 60 hens and 6 cocks, so you have the whole size. The first thing in the 2017 compendium is the floor, which is 3 m by 3 m, so 9 square metres in all, so you will need at least nine such compartments, not five. The chick room has fewer openings than the breeder compartments, which is the rule the 2017 compendium carries out: a chick room kept warm, and the chick room not being opened to the adults, with the chick room at 50 birds per square metre. The feeders and drinkers are sized at the same size as the troughs for the adults. And remember the ground outside: at least 80 cm wide, 20 cm deep and 10 cm tall, with a turnout, because a closed building with a closed henhouse is one where disease flies in. Take the plan to ICAT.

Then the two sizes do not overlap. The commercial reference's 8 to 10 breeders per square metre calls for 68 square metres, so seven by four is about 91 square metres, with 16 to 21 birds per square metre. The 2017 village compendium's improved family henhouse, by contrast, is built for a population of 60 breeding hens and 6 hens, so 57 to 66 square metres, with 12 to 15 birds per square metre for the breeders and 18 to 20 for the growers, which is a much smaller building. Your scheme is still a larger building than either of them, but it is the one the reference's own figures put to the question, so you should weigh what is happening in your own yard before you commit the rent. Ask ICAT, which is the office for the model that matches your plan to the size of your plot.

If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

per_item.reference: No, the cycles overlap. A bird takes twenty-one days of incubation and then six months to reach sale weight, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock, so no bird goes from egg to sale in two months. Six production cycles a year in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference means six settings running at different stages at the same time: one batch in the incubator or under hens, one in the brooder for its first three weeks, one in the chick room, others in the grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds. That is also why the reference asks for at least five compartments: several ages are on the farm at once by design.

history.content: Six cycles a year means a bird goes from egg to sale in two months.

draws.answer: The figure is about a bird, not about a cycle, and I will not put a month on it. What it does give you is a window of two months from the time it is set, so a batch is ready and ready to move, which is what the cycle is built on. It also gives you a figure to compare against. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, which is the official reference for commercial local hens, sets six production cycles a year, eggs about ten days, a hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent, in 2020 prices. It does not give sales, and I will not put a month on that either, because a month is not the whole cycle. ICAT holds the reference and can work it for you with your own prices.

Six cycles a year means a bird goes through six different stages of development in the same year. The six stages are: a hen is laying at 60 to 72 days, an egg is laid in about 21 days, a brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs, a chick hatches in 21 days, a chick goes off feed for the first three weeks, and a grown bird weighs 5.5 kg in all. All of it is laid in one year, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference.

per_item.reference: Look under the leaves of your tomato plants every week to detect any tiny insects. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide on any spray. If the insects are numerous, prune the most infested leaves and destroy them. Remove weeds from the plot edges that can serve as a refuge for the pests. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong water jet to wash off aphids, while ladybirds and lacewings will naturally suppress them. For the approved product and dosage, contact ICAT.

history.content: The leaves on my tomatoes are yellowing and I hear a faint buzzing, what's the first thing I should do?

draws.answer: First, turn the leaves over and count the tiny insects on the underside of a few tomato plants to determine the pest level. Shake each plant and look before you treat, because the wrong name and the wrong product waste your money. If the count is high, pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and clear weeds around the plot. Use yellow sticky traps if whiteflies are present, or spray a strong jet of water and let ladybirds and lacewings help if aphids are present. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. You can see ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

The symptoms you are seeing are from tomato sucking pests, so start by shaking the plant and looking at the underside of the leaves for insects. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. Use yellow sticky traps if whiteflies are present, or apply a strong jet of water to remove aphids and let ladybirds and lacewings help. If the pest pressure is high, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

per_item.reference: From the Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices. Year one, improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, a hungry plant that consumes a lot, maize, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes for the nutrients left deeper, yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year one with legumes. Before fixing it, take account of your soil's fertility and of last season's crop.

history.content: rotation 4 ans exemple

draws.answer: Year one, improving plants: legumes such as groundnut, cowpea or groundnut, which the catalogue calls improving plants, because they are able to live on nitrogen fixed by their root nodules; year two, maize. Year three, a hungry plant such as maize or cowpea, the one that needs the nitrogen. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a root or tuber crop such as yam. The catalogue gives no number of years, no cost and no yield gain for this sequence, so I will not invent one.

Year one: beans, the ones that grow quickly, and the improved varieties of 90 to 95 days, such as Amen, FCMM 18 to 21, Ikenne 11 to 15. Year two: maize, the one the table calls a hungry plant that takes a lot, and the shorter varieties of 55 to 60 days, such as Pool 18 QPM, ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka. Year three: a legume that the soil returns nitrogen to, such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean. Year four: maize then the legumes again. The order is maize at the head, then a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow.

per_item.reference: Transplant seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery, placing 2 to 3 plants per pocket spaced 20 by 20 centimetres. For lowland or irrigated fields, apply 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 about a week after transplanting, then split 100 kilograms per hectare of urea, giving half at tillering and half at panicle initiation. Weed the field at 15 to 25 days after transplanting and again around 40 days. Protect the crop from birds from flowering until harvest. If you need variety matching or rate adjustments, see ICAT.

history.content: How should I transplant and fertilise my rice seedlings?

draws.answer: Transplant the rice seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery. Place two to three rice plants in each pocket that is 20 by 20 centimetres. About seven days after transplanting apply the NPK 15-15-15 at 200 kilograms per hectare in a pocket, then later apply urea at 100 kilograms per hectare in two equal doses, one at the tillering stage and one at panicle initiation. Weed the field first at 15-25 days after transplanting and again at about 40 days. Keep birds away from the crop from flowering until you harvest. For variety matching or rate adjustments, see ICAT.

Transplant your rice seedlings after about 21 days, putting two to three plants in each pocket spaced 20 by 20 cm. Apply NPK 15-15-15 at 200 kg per hectare in a pocket, then split urea at 50 kg per hectare, and earth up against lodging. Keep the second weeding 10-15 days after transplanting and spray an approved fungicide at the labelled rate when birds or wind spread spores. For a soil-specific fertiliser adjustment, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not a pest problem; the maize is experiencing nitrogen depletion on a soil that has lost organic matter. First, look at the leaves: uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves indicates nitrogen hunger. Second, avoid buying a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide based on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on exhausted soil. Third, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the proper dose for your plot. ICAT is the service to see.

history.content: My old maize field in Kara shows pale yellow older leavees while the new ones stay green, is it a pest?

draws.answer: The pale yellow of the older lower leaves of your maize field indicates a nitrogen shortage, not a pest or disease. Begin by reading the leaves: the uniform pale colour on the older lower leaves shows the plant is hungry for nitrogen. Do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide because they will not solve the shortage on their own. Instead, add organic matter such as manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Then plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, request a soil analysis from ICAT to get the proper fertilizer dose for your plot.

Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide based on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on depleted soil. Restore organic matter first by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. After that, include a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. per_item.reference: Then the count against the floor may be fine and the compartment still wrong. Check the number first: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 12 to 15 growers and 50 chicks, so measure and divide before anything else. If you are inside the figure, look at why one end is unused. The reference wants the henhouse well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind, so a cold or wet end will empty. Check the feeders and drinkers are spread rather than grouped: for adults, one feeder of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 birds, and four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred layers. And keep the compartments to their ages, since that is what the five compartment plan is for.

history.content: The birds are crowded at one end and the other end stays empty.

draws.answer: The other end is empty because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts a fenced run around the henhouse, not a fence. The 2017 ESFT village compendium gives it as 3 m by 3 m for a flock of 60 breeding hens, and it says that keeping the birds from crowding lets you watch health and feeding closely. It also says the same about a run: a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one, and it lets you watch the birds better. If you want to build a run, the 2017 compendium gives a structure of at least five compartments, with a grassy run around the henhouse.

That is the edge of the compartment the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for, and it is the one to take aim at. It says you should build the henhouse in such a way that the breeder, the grower and the droffer are all in the same building, and it gives three reasons: keeping disease away, being able to count the eggs and the droppings, and selling the cockerels. The end of the building stays empty because you cannot see what is happening inside: a hen in lay stays in it for twelve months, with a natural hatching rate near seventy percent. Tell the others to go inside as well, because the 2017 ESFT village compendium says the same in its own words: it is easier to adjust the flock to the building than to change it.

per_item.reference: The symptom is nitrogen loss in maize, not a disease that requires roguing. Start by opening a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. When the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burn. Continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as scheduled. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, you should see ICAT.

history.content: After a heavy shower my corn's lower leaves are pale, especially where water pooled. Should I remove the plants?

draws.answer: The pale lower leaves of your maize after heavy rain are a sign of nitrogen loss. Begin by opening a shallow drainage channel so water can run off the plot instead of remaining. When the soil has drained, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying roughly 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer away from the plant to prevent burning. Then keep the second weeding and earthing-up on their planned dates. If streaks or dead-hearts appear, you should consult ICAT.

The pale colour of the lower maize leaves after a heavy rain is due to nitrogen loss, so you should not remove the plants. Begin by opening a shallow drainage channel to let excess water run off the field. Once the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each maize stem, applying about 100 kg per hectare at the panicle initiation stage, and keep the fertilizer away from the plant to prevent burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on their normal timetable. If you notice any streaks on the leaves or dead-heart symptoms, go to ICAT for assistance.

per_item.reference: It is bloat affecting your nanny goat. Immediately get the goat on its feet and keep it moving, holding its head raised to help belching. After that, drench a little vegetable or mineral oil into its mouth to break the froth and free the gas. This helps the rumen work again and lets the gas escape. The condition can lead to collapse very quickly. Call the veterinary service immediately for emergency assistance.

history.content: My nanny goat's left flank is tight, she stopped grazing and looks like she is struggling to breathe.

draws.answer: It is bloat in your nanny goat. First get the goat up and moving, keeping its head raised so it can belch the gas. Then drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the frothy foam in the rumen. This helps the rumen expand and let the gas escape. Call the veterinary service right away because severe bloat needs professional help. The veterinary service is the right place to see for this emergency.

Your nanny goat is experiencing bloat and needs urgent action. Quickly get the goat standing and walking, keeping its head raised to promote belching. Drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth and allow the gas to escape. Call the veterinary service immediately because a severe case requires their intervention without delay. The veterinary service should be contacted immediately.

per_item.reference: Your cattle have gall sickness (anaplasmosis). Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine is yellow-brown without red, which points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade, give it clean water within reach, and do not make it walk because it lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, to stop further spread. See the veterinary service the same day.

history.content: My cows are looking weak, they have yellow urine and seem to lag behind the herd.
Are the gums and eyelids pale or white?
Yes, their gums and eyelids are pale.

draws.answer: Your cattle have gall sickness caused by Anaplasma marginale. Call the veterinary service the same day and tell them the urine colour is yellow-brown without red. Keep the sick animals in shade, provide clean water and do not make them walk. Hand-pick all visible ticks on every animal in the herd, not only on the sick ones. The veterinary service will identify the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Never reuse a needle between animals. You should see the veterinary service the same day.

Your cattle have nagana, a trypanosomiasis spread by tsetse fly bites. Report the problem to the veterinary service for a proper diagnosis and the correct trypanocide; do not guess a drug or dose. Reduce fly exposure by avoiding grazing in riverine bush during biting hours and consider fly control measures. Keep the animals well fed and watered so they can withstand the disease and recover. For diagnosis and treatment, see the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: Waiting with a small bag of beans after the harvest can be profitable. First, make sure the beans are stored well dried to keep them in good condition. Then keep that bag instead of selling the whole harvest immediately. When the lean season arrives, roughly June through August, prices usually go up. Check the weekly market day for your village and follow SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you decide to sell. Compare the local price plus transport cost with the price you might achieve in Lomé or other large markets. If you can, join a cooperative or sell together to reach larger buyers and cut per-bag transport cost. For more assistance, approach a cooperative or ICAT, and also ANSAT for grain.

history.content: I have a small bag of beans left after harvest. Is it smart to wait before selling?

draws.answer: The brochure does not say, and it is fair, so I will not guess at a number. What it tells you to weigh is that you should be selling at the moment when the price is right and that you should follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio before you decide. Two things about the beans. Beans are usually cheap in the lean season, roughly from June to August, so you should be looking before that. And the study's own figures are not in it: 210,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, in 2005 prices. So the bag may be cheap now, but not always. Ask a cooperative or ICAT which of its outlets are open, and ask ANSAT for cereal prices.

Waiting before you sell gives you time to find buyers and raises the price you can receive for your beans. The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure says plainly that keeping them past the harvest season lets you sell them dearer when the time comes. One study puts the result at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags. Write your own figure on the price you can get this season, and compare it with what SIM radios broadcast on the market day. Do not wait for the first price when you hear it: the market price is what you will receive after you have found it.
